job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 (manager's amendment of Oct. 6, 2026): loophole and drafting review

I've ordered these by section. The most serious ones are flagged **[Critical]**. Some items are policy choices rather than drafting errors, and I've noted where I think that's the case.

## Section 2 (Definitions)

1. **§2(1)(A), volume threshold.** Anything at or below 10,000 metric tons per year per vessel is not "commercial," so pilot or "test" mining could continue indefinitely. A company can also split production across several vessels, each under the cap. **[Critical]**
2. **§2(1)(A), "per year" and "metric tons."** The text doesn't say whether "year" means a calendar year, a rolling 12 months, or a license year. It also doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry. Polymetallic nodules carry substantial moisture, so this changes whether a vessel crosses the line.
3. **§2(1)(A), "recovery," "seabed," and "other mineral resources" are undefined.** It's unclear whether in-situ extraction, sediment plumes, seabed-based collectors, or removal from the subsoil count. It's also unclear whether massive sulfides and cobalt crusts are covered, and "other mineral resources" is open to narrowing arguments.
4. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** Collectors, crawlers, risers, or platforms that aren't "vessels" fall outside the literal text. Rotating or chartering vessels can also be used to stay under the per-vessel number.
5. **§2(1)(A), 200-meter depth.** The text doesn't say how or where depth is measured, which invites disputes at the margin. Activity shallower than 200 m is entirely outside the Act, which may or may not be intended.
6. **§2(1)(B), catch-all depends on an undefined "Secretary."** The bill never identifies which Secretary (Commerce? Interior?). The Secretary also isn't required to make any determination, so the catch-all may never be used. **[Critical]**
7. **§2(1)(B), vagueness and delegation.** "Risks... comparable to" is a vague standard with no criteria, procedure, or publication requirement. Because §5(b) attaches criminal liability, a defendant could raise fair-notice, vagueness, and nondelegation challenges. A rule-of-lenity argument is also likely.
8. **§2(2), "U.S. person" is too narrow.** It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other non-"corporation" entities. It also omits corporations organized under DC, territorial, or federal law, and U.S. nationals and permanent residents.
9. **§2(2), foreign subsidiaries.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary of a U.S. parent is not a "U.S. person," and the text has no control, ownership, or financing test. Companies can restructure offshore and keep operating. **[Critical]**
10. **§2(3), "covered vessel" threshold.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less avoid the registry entirely. The 5,000 GT line also doesn't match the 10,000-ton recovery threshold, so a smaller vessel can exceed the recovery cap and never be registered. "Equipped for the recovery" is also undefined.

## Section 3 (Prohibition)

11. **§3(a), "in the United States" is undefined.** The text doesn't say whether it includes the EEZ, the extended continental shelf, territories, or U.S.-flag vessels. "Person" is also undefined, though 1 U.S.C. §1 supplies a default definition.
12. **§3(a), scope is limited to "engaging in" mining.** Nothing prohibits processing, transporting, importing, selling, financing, insuring, or supplying vessels or equipment for deep-sea mining. A foreign operator can mine and sell into the U.S. market or use U.S. processing. This is partly a policy choice, but it's a major gap relative to CADM's goals.
13. **§3, no interaction with existing law.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or override the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act or OCSLA authorities. Agencies could keep accepting applications and issuing licenses or permits, and the Act's relationship to them would be litigated. Please have counsel confirm the exact statutory citations.
14. **§3(b), grandfather clause is open-ended.** It exempts "mining" under any pre-enactment exploration license, with no end date, volume cap, scope limit, or conditions. It doesn't address renewals, extensions, modifications, transfers, or expansion of licenses. **[Critical]**
15. **§3(b), license/permit mismatch.** Exploration licenses are generally not authorizations for commercial recovery, yet the text exempts "mining" conducted under them. That's ambiguous both ways: holders may claim a right to mine commercially, and the provision may be read to cover only exploration. **[Critical]**
16. **§3(b), race to license.** The cutoff is the date of enactment, and the Act doesn't take effect for 180 days. That creates an incentive to rush license issuance or approvals before enactment. Pending applications and the license's issuing authority (U.S. or foreign) aren't addressed.
17. **§3(b), heading versus text.** The heading says "Existing operations," but the text turns on a license, not an operation. Operations without a license, or begun after enactment but before the effective date, have no clear treatment.
18. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** "For the purpose of environmental assessment" is undefined, self-certified, and has no volume cap, permit, duration limit, or ban on commercial sale. Operators could label bulk sampling or test mining as "assessment." **[Critical]**
19. **§3(b)-(c), burden of proof.** The text doesn't say whether these are exemptions the defendant must prove or elements the government must disprove. That affects enforcement in both civil and criminal cases.

## Section 4 (Registry)

20. **§4, no deadline, content, or rulemaking authority.** The text gives no registration deadline, required information, or authority for NOAA to issue regulations. It also doesn't say whether the registry is public.
21. **§4(b), reporting has no teeth.** There's no verification standard, audit or inspection authority, recordkeeping requirement, or required data (volumes, locations, dates). "Certified by the operator" is undefined.
22. **§4, no specific penalty.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or report has no stated consequence. "Operator" is also undefined.

## Section 5 (Penalties)

23. **§5(a), no enforcing agency or procedure.** The text doesn't designate who assesses penalties (Commerce, Coast Guard, DOJ) or provide notice, hearing, or judicial review procedures. It also provides no injunctive relief, no vessel or mineral seizure or forfeiture, and no citizen-suit provision. **[Critical]**
24. **§5(a) vs. §8, internal conflict.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §3 isn't effective until 180 days later. Either the language is surplusage or it creates a retroactivity and due-process problem.
25. **§5(a), penalty amount.** The $1,000,000 maximum has no inflation adjustment, and the text doesn't address minimum penalties or disgorgement. It also doesn't address the economics: a ceiling may be small relative to operating revenue.
26. **§5(b), "willfully."** The text doesn't clarify whether the defendant must know the conduct is unlawful or merely know the underlying facts. Combined with the vague §2(1)(B) standard, this invites a lack-of-notice defense. Imprisonment also doesn't reach corporations, and there's no provision on officer liability.

## Section 6 (International agreement)

27. **§6, hortatory and ambiguous.** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no enforceable duty. It's unclear whether the 18-month deadline is for starting or concluding negotiations. There's no reporting requirement to Congress, and "equivalent to section 3" would import the §3(b)-(c) loopholes into any treaty.

## Section 7 (Duration)

28. **§7(b) contradicts §7(a).** §7(a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress finds mining can be done without serious harm, but §7(b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. The prohibition lapses automatically, and measured from enactment (not the effective date) the real duration is about 9.5 years. **[Critical]**
29. **§7(b), no savings clause.** The text doesn't preserve penalties or liability for violations committed before the sunset. The general saving statute (1 U.S.C. §109) may not clearly apply to expiration, so I'd have counsel check this.
30. **§7(a), standard and mechanism.** "Serious harm" is undefined and weaker than the "irreversible" harm standard that drives CADM's position. NASEM has no mandate or funding to produce the report, and the report isn't binding. It's also unclear whether a finding in a joint resolution automatically ends the prohibition or whether further legislation is needed.

## Section 8 (Effective date) and general

31. **§8, 180-day delay.** This creates a window to begin operations, obtain licenses, or stockpile before the ban applies. It also sets up possible vested-rights or takings arguments. Consider a shorter delay or an immediate stop on new licenses and permits.
32. **Missing boilerplate.** The bill has no severability clause, findings section (which helps defend against commerce, foreign-affairs, and vagueness challenges), regulatory authority, or appropriations authorization. It also has no statement on preemption or on its relationship to other laws.
33. **Extraterritorial reach.** Applying the ban to U.S. persons "anywhere" is defensible, but the bill gives no jurisdictional hook for foreign vessels or entities. Combined with the narrow §2(2), enforcement against offshore operators would be difficult.

## Suggested priorities for markup

If you can only push a few amendments, I'd focus on these:
- **Sunset and duration (#28):** strike or fix §7(b) so it doesn't contradict §7(a).
- **Grandfather clause (#14-16):** cap and condition §3(b), and freeze new licenses.
- **Environmental assessment exemption (#18):** define it narrowly, with a cap and a no-sale rule.
- **U.S. person and foreign subsidiary coverage (#8-9):** broaden the definition and add control or financing tests.
- **Enforcement (#23-24):** designate the agency, procedures, and remedies, and fix the §5(a)/§8 date conflict.
- **Thresholds and catch-all (#1, #6-7):** close the splitting and pilot-scale gaps and make the Secretary's authority defined and mandatory.

I can draft amendment language for any of these if that would help.
